title: Copying Python Lists
learningObjectives: Explain the behavior of copying python lists.
Select appropriate list operations for a given task.
Predict the effect of indexing, mutation and copying.
Write readable code that processes list data.
Avoid common list-related errors and side effects.

understand.concept: Assigning a list to another variable creates another reference to the same list; it does not copy the list. A shallow copy can be made with copy(), list(existing), or a full slice. A shallow copy creates a new outer list but keeps references to nested objects. Use copy.deepcopy when an independent recursive copy of nested mutable objects is required.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding copies prevents accidental changes to data that another part of a program expects to remain unchanged.
understand.analogy: An alias is a second label on the same box; a shallow copy is a new box containing references to the same inner items.
understand.analogyLimit: A shallow copy is not a deep copy. Nested mutable objects may still be shared between the original and its shallow copy.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Assignment creates an alias

`second = first` makes both names refer to the same list object.

## 2. Shallow copies

Use `first.copy()`, `list(first)` or `first[:]` to create a new outer list.

## 3. Nested objects

A shallow copy does not recursively copy nested lists or dictionaries. Changes to a shared nested object can be visible through both lists.

## 4. Deep copy

The copy module provides `deepcopy` for recursively copying nested objects when that behavior is required.

examples.title: Assignment creates an alias
examples.explanation: Both names refer to the same list, so a change through second is visible through first.

examples.title: Use copy method
examples.code:
first = [1, 2]
second = first.copy()
second.append(3)
print(first)
print(second)
examples.explanation: copy creates a separate outer list.

examples.title: Use list constructor
examples.explanation: list(original) creates a shallow copy with a separate outer list.

examples.title: A slice makes a shallow copy
examples.explanation: A full slice creates a new outer list.

examples.title: Nested items remain shared in a shallow copy
examples.explanation: The outer lists differ, but the nested list is shared.

practise.guidedTask: Create a list and assign it to a second name. Show that a mutation affects both names, then use copy() to create an independent outer list.
practise.independentTask: Copy a nested list using copy() and demonstrate the shared inner reference. Then use copy.deepcopy and compare the behavior.
hints: Assignment creates another reference, not a copy.
list(existing) and existing[:] also create shallow copies.
Nested mutable items remain shared in shallow copies.
Use copy.deepcopy for recursive copying when needed.
practise.challenge: Draw a reference diagram for an original list, an alias, a shallow copy and a deep copy. Predict which mutations are visible through each reference.

questions.prompt: What does second = first do when first is a list?
options: Creates another reference to the same list
questions.answer: Creates another reference to the same list
questions.explanation: Assignment binds another name to the same list object.

questions.prompt: Which method makes a shallow list copy?
questions.explanation: The copy method creates a new outer list.

questions.prompt: Are nested lists copied recursively by list.copy()?
questions.explanation: copy creates a shallow copy; nested objects remain shared.

questions.prompt: Which module function makes a deep copy?
questions.explanation: deepcopy recursively copies nested objects according to the copy protocol.
